Hello, I'm Jiho Lee from Team CCGN. This is a one-person project developed with the help of AI coding assistants.

In October, I presented the use case and architecture. Today, I'll show the working prototype, the measurement results, and the integration test with the real ETSI MEC Sandbox.

Before the demo, I'll briefly explain the problem, the goal, and what I built.

IoT devices often have limited resources for running security software. Sending all their data to the cloud for analysis adds communication delays and moves raw data off site.

The goal is to monitor device behavior at the edge and respond using standard oneM2M access control.

The prototype uses tinyIoT as the CSE, a detector registered as a oneM2M AE, a dashboard showing each step, and MEC011 and MEC013 integration.

No additional security software needs to be installed on the devices. They use their existing oneM2M interface, and the platform itself enforces the access restrictions.

The demo uses a smart building scenario, with sensors connected to a oneM2M platform on an on-site MEC server.

The temperature sensor is compromised. It floods the platform with requests, sends abnormal readings, and tries to read the door sensor's data.

The detector runs on the same edge host and records alerts for these behaviors. When it detects a flood, it updates the ACP to block that sensor's access.

It also queries the MEC location service, so the operator can identify the device, see which service is affected, and check its associated location.

This diagram shows the implemented system. On the left are two simulated sensors and an attack tool; the dashed box is one MEC host.

Device requests pass through a request logger, which forwards them to tinyIoT and gives the detector a record of each request. tinyIoT also notifies the detector of every new reading. The detector answers with oneM2M requests, and uses the MEC platform for service discovery and location.

Compared with the interim plan, tinyIoT is now the main CSE, and the dashboard uses Flask.

The project uses oneM2M to store sensor data, deliver notifications, and control access.

Each sensor and the detector register as AEs. The detector checks registered identities to identify requests from an unknown originator.

Sensor readings are stored as content instances inside containers on the edge CSE. The detector subscribes to the temperature container, so the CSE sends it each new reading.

Access control policies determine who can read or write a resource. The detector updates the policy to block a device, then checks for response code 4103 to confirm that the CSE denies access.

Alerts are also stored as content instances, so other oneM2M applications can retrieve them with the appropriate access permissions.

The architecture follows deployment Option D from oneM2M TR-0080. Both the CSE and the detector are applications on the MEC host, and they communicate with the MEC platform over Mp1.

I chose Option D to keep data storage, detection, and access control on the same edge node. This keeps the detection and blocking process within the host.

The integration uses two standard APIs.

With MEC011, the CSE helper application registers the CSE as a service. The detector discovers that service and uses the returned address for its oneM2M requests. It also publishes an alert service that another MEC application can discover.

With MEC013, the detector looks up where the device is attached after blocking its access.

The demo uses the real ETSI MEC Sandbox for these platform APIs.

Let's follow a single sensor reading.

The sensor sends a oneM2M CREATE request through the request logger. The logger records the originator, the requested operation, and the CSE's response. tinyIoT stores the reading as a content instance.

The CSE then notifies the detector through the subscription. The detector analyses the reading on the edge host.

The detector sends its responses back through oneM2M, either by storing an alert or, for a request flood, updating the ACP.

The sensor data stays on the edge host throughout this process. Storage, analysis, and access enforcement all take place locally.

This slide shows what happens during a flood, using results from the run connected to the ETSI MEC Sandbox.

The burst of requests passes through the logger and targets the temperature container in tinyIoT.

When the detector counts more than twelve requests from the sensor within two seconds, it removes the sensor's permission from the temperature policy.

tinyIoT then denies that sensor's access, while the door sensor continues working.

The detector also queries MEC013. For the device identity assigned in this demo, the API returns user equipment 10.1.0.1, in zone03, attached to 4g-macro-cell-6.

This diagram shows the same flood as a sequence of calls.

In step one, the temperature sensor sends a burst of RETRIEVE requests through the logger, which forwards them to tinyIoT.

In step two, the logger passes each request record to the detector.

In step three, the request count exceeds twelve within two seconds, triggering the flood rule.

Steps four to six are oneM2M requests from the detector to the CSE. It stores an alert, removes the sensor's permission from the ACP, and sends a RETRIEVE request using the sensor's identity. The CSE returns 4103, confirming that access is denied.

In step seven, the detector queries MEC013 for the device's associated location.

In step eight, subsequent requests from the temperature sensor are denied, while requests from the door sensor still succeed.

For this prototype, I used simulated oneM2M devices rather than physical hardware. They send the same types of requests that a physical device would send.

The temperature sensor, Ctemp, creates content instances containing temperature readings. In the normal scenario, it sends six readings around 23 degrees Celsius, about a third of a second apart. Each reading reaches the detector through the subscription.

Both sensors also read their own containers once per second. These checks allow the dashboard to show whether each service is accessible.

The attack tool runs in a separate terminal and acts as a compromised device.

The Isolation Forest model is trained on synthetic readings around 23 degrees. A physical board using oneM2M over HTTP could replace Ctemp through the same interface, without changing the CSE or MEC integration. Real sensor data would also be needed for training.

To verify the result, we read the state directly from tinyIoT.

After the flood, the temperature sensor's permission is no longer present in the temperature policy. The detector's alert is also stored as a content instance.

The ETSI MEC Sandbox location API returns the location associated with the sensor's assigned identity: user equipment 10.1.0.1, zone03, and 4g-macro-cell-6.

The service checks confirm the effect of the policy change. The temperature sensor's access is denied, while the door sensor continues working.

Each scenario was repeated thirty times on one PC with tinyIoT.

From the request that crosses the flood threshold to the CSE acknowledging the ACP update, the median was 40.8 milliseconds, and the 95th percentile 79.7.

The block is not instant: in a fast burst, about eight more requests got through first.

These are single-PC figures; they do not show distributed performance.

[If asked: a reading takes about 38 ms to reach a model decision; ACME on the same PC blocks in about 61 ms.]

The model was evaluated offline using synthetic temperature data. The experiment was repeated thirty times, with different random seeds for the training data, normal readings, and attack readings.

The range rule alone detected the temperature spike. Adding Isolation Forest also detected the larger shift, the smaller shift of two and a half standard deviations, and the gradual drift.

However, it also produced an average of 1.26 false alerts per minute on normal data.

I then tested a variation that requires two consecutive AI anomaly flags. This reduced false alerts to 0.03 per minute, while detecting 95.3 percent of the small-shift episodes.

That variation was only tested offline and is not included in the running detector.

The evaluation uses a single temperature feature and synthetic Gaussian data, so these results do not establish accuracy with real sensor data.

On November 17, I ran the integration check against the real ETSI MEC Sandbox.

Over MEC011, the test registered the CSE as a service, discovered it, and retrieved a oneM2M resource through the discovered address. It did the same for the alert service, then removed everything it created.

The endpoints were loopback addresses, so this verifies API integration, not application hosting.

Compared with the interim plan, the core flow, the four threat scenarios, Isolation Forest, verified ACP blocking and the MEC011 services are all delivered, and MEC013 location was added. The detector also runs unchanged on ACME.

I used Flask instead of Streamlit and dropped the humidity sensor; the stretch goals remain future work.

The prototype has four main limitations.

First, an originator string does not authenticate a device. The detector cannot identify an attacker simply copying a valid registered ID.

Second, requests sent directly to the CSE bypass the request logger. Notification-based detection can still analyse newly stored sensor readings, but request-log-based detection misses that traffic.

Third, the measurements come from one PC, one simulated temperature sensor, and synthetic training data.

Fourth, the MEC tests verify API integration using loopback endpoints.

Also, an ACP update denies access to resources, but it does not stop network traffic from reaching the CSE.

The prototype uses oneM2M resources and MEC service APIs to detect four types of abnormal device behavior.

In the local tests, it blocked a flooding sensor's access in about 41 milliseconds after the flood threshold was exceeded. The block was then verified using the CSE's response.

The next steps are to authenticate device identities, add a filter to reduce false alerts, and evaluate the detector with more sensors and real data. I also plan to deploy the CSE and detector as hosted MEC applications.
